dossier.public_summary: The 590 ppm dimming is only seen clearly in two of eight transits and varies from ~800 ppm to undetected across sectors, even within the same data pipeline. A real planet should have a stable depth, so this looks like a few noisy or systematics-driven dips rather than a planet. No companion eclipse is detected, but depth instability is itself positive evidence the signal is not on-target.

reasons.why: Depth changes dramatically between sectors within the same pipeline product, from undetected (~91 ppm, consistent with zero) to ~1694 ppm. Many real planets show only calibration differences between products; this is true change within TESS-SPOC.
reasons.value: verdict=changes_within_a_source, p_constant_all=1.880436183597206e-15, TESS-SPOC p_constant=2.245374385648822e-11, per-sector 805, 1694, 91, 255, 1333 ppm, depth_change_pct=191.8%

reasons.why: Two of the eight events carry almost all the signal; most transits near zero. A planet should give consistent depths, but this is driven by a few anomalous deep dips.
reasons.value: 8 transits, p_consistent=1.2992852441656772e-20, chi2=109.27 dof=7, share_of_top_3=0.965, outliers 1694 ppm (sigma=6.7) and 1282 ppm (sigma=4.2) at epochs -47 and -48, mean 587 ppm

reasons.why: Statistically decisive depth instability between sectors, not explained by TESS-SPOC vs SPOC differences alone.

Flat-bottomed small-planet size and no strong secondary and no odd/even difference argue for a planet, but this clean-dip signature does not overcome the positive false-alarm evidence of depth variation and outlier-driven significance.
